turns.text:
# Room-by-Room Packing Checklist: Kitchen & Living Room

---

## KITCHEN

The kitchen takes the longest and breaks the most stuff. Start here early — you use fewer kitchen items daily than you think.

**Estimated total time:** 8–12 hours across multiple sessions

---

### Declutter First (Week 7–6) — **J**, 2–3 hrs

Go through every drawer and cabinet once before you touch a box. For each item, ask: *Have we used this in the last year? Can we replace it for under $20 in Oregon? Are we keeping duplicates?*

Common kitchen cuts that save real weight and box space: mismatched tupperware and lids (keep only nesting sets), chipped mugs and glasses, duplicate spatulas and wooden spoons, expired spices and pantry items (check the shelf — most people find 10–15 expired items), single-use gadgets you bought optimistically (bread maker, fondue pot, spiralizer), old cookbooks you haven't opened (photograph favorite recipes instead), and cleaning supplies that are cheaper to rebuy than to move.

Donate or sell anything in good shape. Most Goodwills and Habitat ReStores take kitchen items. Post bigger items on your local Buy Nothing group or Facebook Marketplace. For hazardous items like propane, lighter fluid, and certain cleaners, check your Ohio county's household hazardous waste drop-off — movers won't take them and they can't go in a truck safely.

---

### Pack in Three Waves

**Wave 1: Rarely used items (Weeks 6–5)** — **P**, 3–4 hrs

- [ ] Baking dishes, specialty pans, cake pans, muffin tins
- [ ] Holiday and entertaining dishes, serving platters, punch bowls
- [ ] Small appliances you won't use before the move (stand mixer, blender, food processor, slow cooker, waffle iron)
- [ ] Fine china or fragile glassware (wine glasses, stemware)
- [ ] Cookbooks (keep 1–2 favorites out if you cook from them)
- [ ] Vases, candles, decorative items stored in the kitchen
- [ ] Extra dish towels, tablecloths, cloth napkins

*Packing tip:* Wrap each plate individually in packing paper (not newspaper — the ink transfers). Stack plates vertically like records, not flat. They're stronger on edge. Nest bowls with paper between them. Put a "FRAGILE — THIS SIDE UP" note on every dish box and don't stack heavy boxes on top.

**Wave 2: Most of the kitchen (Week 3–2)** — **P**, 3–4 hrs

- [ ] Most pots and pans (keep one skillet, one saucepan out)
- [ ] Most utensils (keep one chef's knife, one spatula, one wooden spoon, tongs)
- [ ] Most cups and mugs (keep 2 each)
- [ ] Toaster, coffee maker (switch to pour-over or instant for the last week if you can stand it)
- [ ] Cutting boards beyond one
- [ ] Spice rack (tape lids, bag them in a zip-lock in case of leaks, pack upright)
- [ ] Pantry items you're keeping (dry goods, canned items — these are heavy, use small boxes)
- [ ] Drawer organizers, junk drawer contents, rubber bands, twist ties

*Packing tip:* Small boxes for heavy items. A large box full of canned goods can hit 60–70 lbs and will tear or hurt someone. Keep each kitchen box under 30–35 lbs. Fill gaps with dish towels or packing paper so nothing shifts.

**Wave 3: Last-day kitchen (Moving day minus 1)** — **J**, 1–2 hrs

- [ ] Remaining skillet, saucepan, spatula, knife, tongs
- [ ] Last 2 mugs and 2 plates
- [ ] Dish soap, sponge, one hand towel
- [ ] Trash bags (keep a few out — you'll need them on moving day)
- [ ] Paper towels (last roll stays out until the truck is loaded)
- [ ] Remaining cleaning supplies for the final wipe-down

*Label this box "OPEN FIRST — KITCHEN" and put it in the car or last on the truck.*

---

## LIVING ROOM

The living room is usually faster than people expect because so much of it is furniture the movers handle. The real work is the stuff *on* and *around* the furniture.

**Estimated total time:** 5–8 hours across sessions (longer because of your 200 books and the bike)

---

### Declutter First (Week 7–6) — **J**, 2–3 hrs

Books are the big decision here. At roughly 200 volumes, you're looking at 10–13 medium boxes weighing 30–40 lbs each. That's real truck space and real weight on a moving estimate. Some options to consider together: keep the ones that matter to you emotionally, professionally, or that you'll reread; sell or donate the rest. Half Price Books buys in bulk and gives you a quote on the spot. Little Free Libraries, local library donation programs, and Buy Nothing groups move books fast. If you're on the fence about a title, take a photo of the spine and let it go — you can rebuy or borrow later.

Beyond books, common living room cuts include old magazines, dead remotes, cables and chargers for devices you no longer own, board games with missing pieces, DVDs and CDs you've replaced with streaming, throw pillows and blankets that are worn, and decor that doesn't fit the new space.

---

### Pack in Three Waves

**Wave 1: Shelves and storage (Weeks 5–4)** — **M**, 3–4 hrs (books take time)

- [ ] **Books:** Pack in small or medium boxes only — a large box of books is a back injury. Stand hardcovers upright, spine down. Lay paperbacks flat in alternating directions. Fill gaps with packing paper so they don't shift. Label each box "BOOKS — HEAVY" and number them (Books 1 of 13, etc.) so you know if one goes missing.
- [ ] DVDs, CDs, vinyl records, video games
- [ ] Photo albums and framed photos (wrap frames in bubble wrap or towels; put cardboard corners on anything with glass)
- [ ] Board games and puzzles (rubber-band the lids shut)
- [ ] Decorative objects, candles, bookends, sculptures
- [ ] Seasonal items stored in living room closets

**Wave 2: Surfaces and electronics (Week 3–2)** — **M**, 2–3 hrs

- [ ] Lamps (remove bulbs and shades separately; wrap shades in large bags or pillowcases)
- [ ] Electronics: TV, gaming console, speakers, router, streaming devices. Photograph the cable setup behind each device before you unplug anything — you'll thank yourself later. Coil each cable and label it or bag it with the device it belongs to. If you still have original TV or console boxes, use them. If not, get a TV box from a moving supply store or U-Haul — TVs are expensive to replace.
- [ ] Remotes (bag them together, label "LIVING ROOM REMOTES")
- [ ] Throw blankets, decorative pillows you're keeping
- [ ] Side table and coffee table contents (coasters, trays, magazines)
- [ ] Area rugs (roll tightly, secure with packing tape or rope; if they'll be in the truck more than a few days, wrap in plastic to prevent moisture damage)

**Wave 3: Furniture prep (Week 1 / Moving day)** — **J**, 1–2 hrs (or movers handle)

- [ ] **Queen mattress:** Get a mattress bag (around $10–$15 at any moving supply store). Slide it on before it goes in the truck. If you're using movers, they usually provide one — confirm ahead of time. Transport the mattress on its side if possible so it doesn't get crushed under boxes.
- [ ] **Bike:** Remove the front wheel and pedals if you can (5 min with a wrench). Wrap the frame in moving blankets or bubble wrap and secure with tape. If you have a bike box from a shop, use it. If the bike is going in a truck with movers, point it out and ask them to strap it — bikes get damaged easily when they shift. If it's going on a car rack, make sure the rack is rated for highway speeds and cross-country distance.
- [ ] Couch cushions (bag them in large trash bags to keep them clean)
- [ ] Disassemble shelving, media console, and tables if needed. Bag all hardware in a zip-lock and tape it to the furniture piece it belongs to. Keep the Allen wrenches with the hardware.
- [ ] Vacuum and wipe down the empty room before the walk-through

---

## Quick-Reference: Box Counts (Estimates)

| Category | Approx. Boxes | Box Size | Weight per Box |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kitchen dishes and glassware | 4–6 | Medium | 25–35 lbs |
| Kitchen pantry and dry goods | 2–4 | Small | 30–40 lbs |
| Kitchen appliances | 2–3 | Medium/Large | 15–30 lbs |
| Kitchen misc (utensils, towels, etc.) | 2–3 | Medium | 15–25 lbs |
| Books (200 volumes) | 10–13 | Small/Medium | 30–40 lbs |
| Living room decor and media | 3–5 | Medium | 15–25 lbs |
| Electronics | 2–3 | Varies | Varies |
| Lamps and shades | 1–2 | Large | 10–15 lbs |

---

Ready for bedrooms, bathroom, and garage/storage whenever you are. The garage section will also cover general outdoor gear, tools, and anything that movers won't transport (fuel, paint, propane, etc.).

turns.text:
# Room-by-Room Packing Checklist: Bedrooms, Bathroom & Garage/Storage

---

## MASTER BEDROOM

The bedroom feels simple until you open the closets. Clothes and linens are bulky, not heavy, so the challenge is volume, not weight. Your queen mattress is already bagged from the living room prep — good.

**Estimated total time:** 6–9 hours across sessions

---

### Declutter First (Week 7–6) — **J**, 2–3 hrs

Closets are where moves get expensive because you're paying by space or truck footage to haul things you forgot you owned. Pull everything out of both closets and sort into four piles: keep, donate, sell, trash. Some guidelines that help: if you haven't worn it in a year and it doesn't have sentimental or seasonal value, let it go. Shoes you don't love walking in won't improve in Oregon. Stretched-out basics like old t-shirts and underwear are cheaper to replace than to move. Coats and heavy winter gear still matter — Oregon's winters are milder than Ohio's in the valleys but you'll want layers, especially if you're near the mountains or the coast.

For linens, most households have 2–3x more bedding than they use. Keep one set per bed plus one backup. Donate flat or stained pillows, mismatched sheet sets, and the guest bedding you never actually put on a guest bed. Old comforters and blankets in decent shape go fast at donation centers.

Nightstand drawers tend to accumulate cables, old glasses, random batteries, receipts, and half-read books. Empty them completely and only put back what you'd actually set up on a nightstand in the new place.

---

### Pack in Three Waves

**Wave 1: Off-season and storage (Weeks 5–4)** — **P**, 2–3 hrs

- [ ] Off-season clothes (heavy coats if moving in summer, shorts and sandals if winter). Use wardrobe boxes if the budget allows — they keep hanging clothes clean and wrinkle-free and cost about $10–$15 each. You'll need roughly 2–4 depending on how much you kept.
- [ ] Formal wear, suits, dresses you won't wear before the move
- [ ] Extra shoes and boots (stuff socks or packing paper inside each shoe to hold its shape, then pair them in bags)
- [ ] Spare bedding sets, extra pillows, quilts
- [ ] Luggage and duffel bags (pack soft items inside them — they're free boxes)
- [ ] Memorabilia, keepsakes, jewelry you don't wear daily (wrap fine jewelry individually and keep it in your car documents pouch, not the truck)
- [ ] Under-bed storage bins and their contents (sort before repacking)
- [ ] Seasonal decor stored in bedroom closets

*Packing tip:* Dresser drawers full of folded clothes can sometimes stay in the dresser if you're using movers — ask them. If DIY, pull the drawers out and wrap them in stretch wrap to keep the clothes in place, then stack them. This saves boxes and time.

**Wave 2: Most of the closet and surfaces (Week 3–2)** — **P**, 2–3 hrs

- [ ] Most hanging clothes (leave 4–5 days of outfits out). Wardrobe boxes or the trash-bag-over-hangers trick: punch a small hole in the bottom of a large trash bag, slide 8–10 hangers through the hole so the hooks poke out, and tie the bag loosely at the bottom. Keeps clothes clean and together.
- [ ] Most folded clothes from dressers (keep 2 outfits per person out)
- [ ] Most shoes (keep one everyday pair and one weather-appropriate pair out)
- [ ] Mirrors and wall art (wrap in bubble wrap, then sandwich between two pieces of cardboard taped together; label "GLASS" and store vertically in the truck)
- [ ] Alarm clock, fan, humidifier, white noise machine
- [ ] Hamper and iron/ironing board
- [ ] Curtains and rods (if you're taking them — measure the new windows first)
- [ ] Rugs

**Wave 3: Bedside kits and final strip (Moving day minus 1)** — **J**, 1–1.5 hrs

- [ ] Strip the bed. The mattress is already bagged. Roll sheets and the last pillowcase into a bag.
- [ ] **Keep one bedside kit per person — do not pack these. They go in the car:**
  - Phone charger and backup battery
  - Current medications and vitamins (with original labels)
  - 2 changes of clothes (one for travel, one for arrival day)
  - Toothbrush, deodorant, face wash (small bag)
  - Glasses or contacts and solution
  - Sleep essentials if you're staying in hotels: earplugs, eye mask, melatonin if you use it
- [ ] Pack the last pillow per person into the car for road-trip naps — not the truck
- [ ] Disassemble the bed frame. Bag all bolts, screws, and slats hardware in a zip-lock and tape it directly to the frame rail. Keep the Allen key or wrench with it. Photograph the assembly if the frame is complicated.
- [ ] Nightstands: empty the last drawer, wipe down, done
- [ ] Final vacuum and wipe

---

### Guest Bedroom / Office (if applicable)

If you have a second bedroom used as a guest room or office, it usually packs in a single session because there's less daily-use stuff.

**Estimated total time:** 2–4 hours — **M**, all in one session during Week 4–3

- [ ] Desk contents: sort paperwork (shred what you don't need, file what you do into the car documents folder)
- [ ] Computer, monitor, keyboard, mouse (photograph cable setup, coil and label each cable, use original boxes if you have them)
- [ ] Printer (remove ink cartridges and bag them separately — they leak in transit)
- [ ] Office supplies: keep a pen, a notepad, tape, and a marker out until moving day, pack the rest
- [ ] Guest bedding and pillows (donate if worn)
- [ ] Closet overflow: often this is where the random storage lives — holiday decor, luggage, old hobby supplies. Declutter hard here.
- [ ] Bookshelf contents (most books should already be packed from the living room wave)

---

## BATHROOM(S)

Bathrooms are small but deceptively time-consuming because of liquids, sharps, and the sheer number of tiny items crammed under the sink.

**Estimated total time:** 2–3 hours per bathroom

---

### Declutter First (Week 6–5) — **J**, 1 hr per bathroom

The medicine cabinet and under-sink area are the two biggest purge zones in any home. Check expiration dates on everything. Most people find medications, sunscreen, and skincare products that expired 1–3 years ago. Expired medications should go to a pharmacy take-back program or an FDA-approved disposal location, not down the drain or in the trash (some exceptions exist — check FDA guidelines or ask your pharmacist). Expired cosmetics and skincare can go in the trash.

Other common bathroom cuts: hotel shampoo and lotion collections, hair products that didn't work for you, duplicate razors and toothbrushes still in packaging (donate unopened toiletries to a local shelter — they always need them), ratty towels and washcloths beyond what you actually use (keep 2 per person plus 2 for the dog), cleaning supplies that are nearly empty, and the curling iron or styling tool you haven't plugged in since 2021.

---

### Pack in Two Waves

**Wave 1: Cabinets and storage (Week 3–2)** — **M**, 1.5–2 hrs per bathroom

- [ ] Backup toiletries and bulk items (extra shampoo, soap, toothpaste)
- [ ] First aid kit (restock anything missing before you move — you'll want a full kit in the car)
- [ ] Medications you aren't currently taking (keep current prescriptions in your bedside kit)
- [ ] Hair tools you won't use in the next 2 weeks (wrap cords around each tool and rubber-band them)
- [ ] Towels and washcloths beyond your daily set (use them as packing material for fragile items — dual purpose)
- [ ] Bathroom decor, extra mirrors, soap dishes, organizers
- [ ] Cleaning supplies under the sink (see the movers-won't-transport list at the end — some cleaners are restricted)
- [ ] Scale, step stool, trash can

*Packing tip:* Liquids leak. Put every bottle in a zip-lock bag or wrap it in cling wrap with a rubber band over the cap. Pack liquids upright in a small box lined with a trash bag. Label it "LIQUIDS — UPRIGHT" on all sides. Even with precautions, consider whether a half-empty bottle of conditioner is worth the risk to the box of towels beneath it.

**Wave 2: Daily-use strip (Moving day minus 1)** — **J**, 30–45 min

- [ ] Last towels (1 per person for the final shower)
- [ ] Shower curtain and rings (if you're taking them)
- [ ] Toilet paper — keep 2 rolls out until the last moment, then toss them in the car
- [ ] Hand soap
- [ ] Toothbrush, toothpaste, face wash, deodorant, razor — these go in your bedside travel bag, not a box
- [ ] Prescription medications — bedside kit, not a box
- [ ] Final wipe-down of counters, toilet, mirror, floor
- [ ] Plunger and toilet brush: honestly, consider leaving these and buying new ones in Oregon. If keeping, bag them in trash bags.

---

## GARAGE / STORAGE / OUTDOOR

This is where moves stall. Garages accumulate years of "I'll deal with it later" items, and a surprising number of common garage contents are prohibited from moving trucks. Start the garage early and treat it as a major declutter event, not just a packing task.

**Estimated total time:** 8–14 hours (the widest range because garage contents vary enormously)

---

### Declutter First (Week 8–6) — **J**, 3–5 hrs

Walk through the entire garage and sort everything into zones: tools, automotive, sports and outdoor, holiday, chemicals and paint, and "why do we have this." Be ruthless. You're paying per pound or per cubic foot to haul this across the country.

Specific declutter targets: partially used paint cans (take the lids to a paint store and get color-match codes saved to your phone, then dispose of the paint properly through your county's hazardous waste program), old motor oil and automotive fluids (auto parts stores like AutoZone accept used oil for free), broken tools and duplicates, garden hoses and sprinklers that are cracked or leaking, pots with no plants and soil bags, rusty or wobbly shelving, holiday lights that are half-burnt-out, that box of random screws and nails and hardware — keep it if it's organized, dump it if it's chaos.

The bike is already prepped from the living room section (front wheel and pedals removed, frame wrapped).

---

### Pack in Two Waves

**Wave 1: Stored and seasonal items (Weeks 5–4)** — **M**, 3–5 hrs

- [ ] Holiday decorations (consolidate into fewer bins if possible — ornaments get their own small box with dividers or egg-carton-style packing)
- [ ] Camping and outdoor gear: tent, sleeping bags, camp stove (empty fuel canisters completely and do not pack them — see prohibited list), coolers, hiking packs
- [ ] Sports equipment: balls, rackets, golf clubs, skis, snowboard. Wrap heads and blades individually. Golf bags can stay assembled.
- [ ] Lawn and garden tools you're keeping: shovels, rakes, pruners. Bundle long-handled tools together with rope or bungee cords. Clean soil off everything — Oregon has agricultural inspection stations and dirty tools can cause delays or questions.
- [ ] Power tools: drain all fuel from gas-powered tools (mower, leaf blower, chainsaw, trimmer) completely. Even fumes can be a hazard in an enclosed truck. Wrap blades and bits. Coil cords and label.
- [ ] Hand tools: wrenches, screwdrivers, hammer, pliers, socket set. A tool bag or small toolbox keeps these together. Keep one basic set out until moving day (screwdriver, pliers, adjustable wrench, box cutter, tape measure) for furniture disassembly.
- [ ] Workbench contents: sort hardware into labeled bags. Throw away rusted or unidentified fasteners.
- [ ] Luggage and storage bins you didn't already pack from the bedroom
- [ ] Ladders: if full-size, consider whether it's worth moving vs. buying in Oregon. Extension ladders eat truck space.
- [ ] Bike accessories: helmet, pump, lock, lights, panniers — bag together and label

**Wave 2: Final garage items (Week 1)** — **M**, 2–3 hrs

- [ ] Remaining tools (the set you kept out for disassembly goes in the car for reassembly at the new place)
- [ ] Broom and dustpan (last items — you'll sweep the garage floor)
- [ ] Trash cans and recycling bins (empty, clean, usually not worth moving unless they're nice)
- [ ] Garden hose (drain completely, coil, and secure)
- [ ] Grill: clean it out, remove and properly dispose of the propane tank (see below), wrap grates
- [ ] Shelving units: disassemble, bag hardware, label
- [ ] Sweep and photograph the empty garage

---

## ITEMS MOVERS WON'T TRANSPORT

Federal and carrier regulations prohibit these from commercial moving trucks. If you're driving a DIY truck, some of these are still illegal or dangerous to transport. Dispose of them properly before the move.

**Flammable Liquids and Gases**
- Propane tanks (even "empty" ones — exchange or return to a Blue Rhino or AmeriGas location, or check your local fire department's disposal program)
- Gasoline, kerosene, lighter fluid
- Paint thinner, turpentine, mineral spirits, acetone
- Lamp oil

**Paints and Chemicals**
- Latex and oil-based paints (dry latex paint can go in regular trash in many municipalities — mix with cat litter and let it harden, then check local rules)
- Stains and varnishes
- Pesticides, herbicides, fertilizers with chemicals
- Pool chemicals
- Household cleaners containing bleach, ammonia, or acid (some movers allow sealed, consumer-size cleaners — ask yours specifically)

**Automotive**
- Motor oil and transmission fluid (AutoZone, O'Reilly, and similar stores accept used oil)
- Antifreeze
- Brake fluid
- Car batteries (auto parts stores often accept these for recycling)

**Pressurized Containers**
- Aerosol cans of any kind (spray paint, hairspray, cooking spray, WD-40, compressed air dusters)
- Fire extinguishers (some movers accept these — ask, but don't assume)
- CO2 cartridges
- Scuba tanks

**Batteries and Electronics**
- Car batteries (see above)
- Loose lithium batteries (tape terminals and keep them with you if you need to transport them)
- Damaged or swollen lithium batteries (do not transport — take to a battery recycling drop-off like Call2Recycle locations at Lowe's, Home Depot, or Best Buy)

**Explosives and Ammunition**
- Firearms ammunition (transport in your personal vehicle following federal and state laws for each state you pass through — research Ohio, Indiana/Illinois/Iowa or whichever route you take, Nebraska/Wyoming, and Oregon laws individually, or ship via a licensed dealer)
- Fireworks
- Flares

**Perishable and Living**
- Perishable food (opened, refrigerated, or frozen — eat it, give it away, or toss it)
- Plants (many movers won't take them, and Oregon has border agricultural inspection that may confiscate certain plants, soil, or produce — check the Oregon Department of Agriculture's guidelines)
- Live animals (obviously — the dog rides with you)

**Other**
- Nail polish and nail polish remover (flammable)
- Rubbing alcohol in large quantities
- Charcoal and charcoal lighter
- Oxygen tanks

turns.text:
# Room-by-Room Packing Checklist: Office, Attic/Basement, Outdoor & Misc Storage

---

## HOME OFFICE

The office is where your most valuable and irreplaceable items live — not in dollar terms necessarily, but in data, documents, and devices that can't be re-bought at a store in Oregon. The packing itself is straightforward; the preparation and backup work is what takes time.

**Estimated total time:** 5–8 hours (including digital backup and document sorting)

---

### Electronics Backup Protocol (Week 6–5) — **J**, 2–3 hrs

Do this before you pack a single cable. Moving is the highest-risk moment for electronics — drops, temperature swings, vibration, and moisture all threaten data. Assume anything could arrive damaged and prepare accordingly.

**Computers (desktop and laptops)**

- [ ] Run a full backup of each computer to an external hard drive. If you already use Time Machine, Windows Backup, or a similar tool, run a fresh one. If you don't, this is the moment to start. Plug in an external drive, run the backup, verify it completed, and label the drive.
- [ ] Run a second backup to a cloud service. If you already use iCloud, Google Drive, OneDrive, or Dropbox, confirm your most important folders are synced and up to date. If you don't use cloud backup, consider a one-month subscription to Backblaze or similar — it's about $7–$9 and covers unlimited data from one computer. The goal is redundancy: one local copy on a drive you carry in the car, one cloud copy that survives even if the drive and the computer are both lost.
- [ ] Photograph your desktop setup from multiple angles: front, back (showing every cable connection), and any peripherals. When you reassemble in Oregon, these photos save an hour of "where did this USB go."
- [ ] Write down or screenshot your Wi-Fi network name, passwords for any network-attached devices (printer, NAS, smart home hub), and any software license keys stored locally. Save this to a note on your phone and to the cloud.

**Phones and tablets**

- [ ] Confirm iCloud or Google backup is current on each phone. Check settings and verify the last backup date.
- [ ] Download offline maps for your driving route in Google Maps or Apple Maps. Cell coverage is spotty in parts of Wyoming, Idaho, and rural Oregon.

**External drives, USBs, and memory cards**

- [ ] Gather all of them in one place. Label each one with its contents if you haven't already. These ride in the car with you, never in the truck.

**Serial numbers and warranty info**

- [ ] Photograph the serial number sticker on the back or bottom of every piece of electronics worth more than $200: computers, monitors, TV (if not already done in living room), gaming consoles, tablets, cameras, printers. Save the photos to a dedicated album on your phone called "Move — Serial Numbers." If anything is lost, damaged, or stolen during the move, you'll need serial numbers for insurance claims and police reports.
- [ ] If you have receipts or warranty documents for major electronics, photograph those too and add them to the same album.

---

### Declutter First (Week 5–4) — **M**, 1–2 hrs

Office clutter tends to be paper and cables. Go through every drawer and shelf and pull out old manuals for products you no longer own, cables and adapters you can't identify (the "mystery cable" drawer is universal — if you can't name what it connects to in 10 seconds, recycle it at a Best Buy or Staples e-waste bin), dried-out pens and markers, old business cards, outdated reference materials, and printed documents you have digital copies of.

For paper files: you'll sort these in detail during the document packing step below. For now, pull out anything that's clearly trash — old bank statements from 5+ years ago that you have digital access to, expired insurance cards, junk mail that migrated into a file folder.

Shred anything with personal information before you toss it. If you don't have a shredder, many UPS Stores and FedEx offices offer shredding by the pound.

---

### Pack in Two Waves

**Wave 1: Non-daily office contents (Week 4–3)** — **M**, 2–3 hrs

- [ ] Reference books and binders (small boxes — these are heavy like the living room books)
- [ ] Printer: remove ink or toner cartridges and bag them in a zip-lock (they leak under pressure and temperature changes). If the printer is more than 3–4 years old and was under $150, consider recycling it and buying new in Oregon — printers are cheap, and old ones often don't survive moves well. Staples and Best Buy accept printers for recycling.
- [ ] Scanner, shredder, label maker, and other peripheral devices
- [ ] Desk lamp (remove bulb, wrap shade)
- [ ] Office supplies: stapler, tape dispenser, paper clips, sticky notes, envelopes, stamps. Consolidate into one box. Keep a pen, a Sharpie, packing tape, scissors, and a notepad out until moving day.
- [ ] Filing cabinet contents: see the document sorting section below. The cabinet itself can go empty — bag the drawer hardware if you're disassembling it.
- [ ] Wall art, diplomas, certificates, bulletin board (wrap framed items as described in bedroom section — cardboard sandwich for glass)
- [ ] Surge protectors and power strips (coil cords and rubber-band them, but do not pack these in the same box as anything fragile — the cords tangle and shift)
- [ ] Networking gear you're replacing (old routers, range extenders, outdated modems — recycle or donate)

**Wave 2: Daily-use electronics and desk (Week 1 / Moving day minus 1)** — **M**, 1–2 hrs

- [ ] Desktop computer: shut it down properly (don't just unplug). If it's a tower, transport it upright if possible, and remove the GPU if it's a heavy aftermarket card — GPUs mounted horizontally in a tower can snap off their PCIe slot during truck vibration. Wrap the tower in a moving blanket. If you have the original box and foam, use them. The monitor gets its own wrap and should be treated like a TV — face it toward a padded surface, never lay it screen-down on a hard box.
- [ ] Laptop: goes in your bag in the car, fully charged, not the truck.
- [ ] Monitor, keyboard, mouse, webcam (label each cable and bag with its device)
- [ ] Router and modem: you may need to return these to your Ohio ISP. Check whether they're rented or owned. If rented, return them before you leave or ship them back — ISPs charge $100–$200 for unreturned equipment.
- [ ] Desk chair: if it's a good ergonomic chair worth keeping, remove the base from the seat (usually one bolt or a lever) so it takes up less truck space. Wrap the arms. If it's a $60 task chair, donate it and get a new one.
- [ ] Desk: if it disassembles, do so. Bag and tape all hardware to the largest piece. If it's a solid slab desk, the movers handle it as furniture.
- [ ] Final sweep of all drawers and cubbies — people leave thumb drives, keys, and cash in desk drawers more often than you'd expect

---

## ATTIC / BASEMENT / CRAWL SPACE

These spaces are where things go to be forgotten, so approach this as an archaeological dig first and a packing job second. If you haven't opened a box since you moved into this house, there's a strong chance you don't need what's inside it.

**Estimated total time:** 4–10 hours (wildly dependent on how much is stored)

---

### Declutter First (Week 8–6) — **J**, 2–4 hrs

This is the highest-impact declutter session of the entire move. Bring trash bags, a donation bin, and your phone (for listing items to sell). Go through everything and ask one question per item: "Would I pay $50 to have this shipped to Oregon?" If the answer is no, it goes.

Common attic and basement cuts: old furniture you replaced and stored "just in case," broken holiday decorations, outgrown clothing in storage bins, old textbooks and school papers (photograph anything sentimental, recycle the rest), luggage with broken wheels or zippers, exercise equipment you haven't used in a year (treadmills and ellipticals are expensive to move and cheap to find used in Oregon on Craigslist or Facebook Marketplace), boxes from previous moves that you never unpacked (if you survived this long without opening them, you don't need what's inside — open them one last time to confirm, then donate or toss), and old electronics like VCRs, ancient laptops, and CRT monitors (e-waste recycling).

**Moisture and pest check:** Before you pack anything from a basement or attic, inspect it. Look for water damage, mold, mildew, mouse droppings, or insect damage. If a box is water-stained, the contents may be compromised. If you find mold on fabric or paper, it's usually not worth saving — mold spores will travel with the item and colonize your new space. If in doubt, photograph the item, discard it, and file an insurance claim on your renter's or homeowner's policy if it's valuable.

---

### Pack in Two Waves

**Wave 1: Keep-and-repack (Weeks 5–4)** — **J**, 2–4 hrs

- [ ] Holiday and seasonal decorations (consolidate — if you have 6 bins of Christmas decorations, can it be 3?)
- [ ] Keepsakes and memorabilia: family photos, yearbooks, heirlooms. Wrap fragile items individually. These go in clearly labeled boxes — "KEEPSAKES — FRAGILE — DO NOT STACK." Consider putting irreplaceable photos and documents in a waterproof bin or bag.
- [ ] Seasonal clothing not already packed from bedroom wave 1
- [ ] Stored luggage and bags (pack soft items inside them)
- [ ] Craft and hobby supplies: sewing machine, fabric, yarn, woodworking project stock. Be selective — raw materials are heavy and cheap to replace.
- [ ] Stored kitchenware and dishes you're keeping (china sets, inherited pieces)
- [ ] Archived paperwork and tax records: keep 3–7 years of tax returns depending on your situation (the IRS generally recommends 3 years minimum, but some advisors suggest 7 for safety). Shred older documents with personal information. See the documents section below for what to carry with you vs. what can go in the truck.
- [ ] Tools and hardware that didn't live in the garage

**Wave 2: Large and awkward items (Week 2–1)** — **M**, 1–2 hrs

- [ ] Folding tables, spare furniture, shelving units (disassemble, bag hardware)
- [ ] Storage racks and bins (empty, nest, and stack)
- [ ] Dehumidifier, space heater, window AC unit (drain all water, coil cords). Note: Oregon's climate may mean you no longer need a dehumidifier or window AC depending on where you're moving — the Willamette Valley is mild, and many homes have central air or don't need it.
- [ ] Washer and dryer connections: if you own them and are moving them, disconnect water lines (shut off water first), drain hoses, and secure the washer drum with transit bolts (check your model's manual — running a washer without transit bolts during a move can destroy the drum suspension). If you don't have the transit bolts, a moving company can sometimes source them, or check the manufacturer's website.
- [ ] Final sweep: flashlight check every corner, shelf, rafter, and crawl space. It's very common to leave things in attic eaves and basement utility closets.

---

## OUTDOOR GEAR & MISCELLANEOUS STORAGE

This covers the porch, patio, shed, balcony, car trunk, and anywhere else items accumulate outside the main rooms.

**Estimated total time:** 3–5 hours

---

### Declutter First (Week 6–5) — **M**, 1–2 hrs

Outdoor items take a beating from weather and are often the least worth moving. Inspect everything for rust, rot, UV damage, and broken parts. Plastic patio furniture that's become brittle and faded is not worth truck space. Clay pots crack easily in transit and are cheap to replace. Garden soil and mulch stay behind — the weight isn't worth it and Oregon's agricultural inspection may flag out-of-state soil anyway.

Keep things that are expensive, in good condition, and that you'll use in Oregon: quality patio set, grill (propane tank disposed of separately — see the prohibited items list in the garage section), good garden tools, outdoor recreation gear.

---

### Pack in One Wave (Weeks 4–3) — **M**, 2–3 hrs

- [ ] Patio furniture: clean, dry, and disassemble if possible. Wrap cushions in plastic bags to protect from moisture in the truck. Stack chairs and bag hardware.
- [ ] Grill: deep clean the grates and interior. Remove and properly dispose of the propane tank. Wrap grates in newspaper or packing paper. Tape the lid shut.
- [ ] Outdoor recreation: kayak, paddleboard, ski gear, fishing rods, camping chairs. Fishing rods should be transported in a hard case or PVC tube — they snap easily. Ski edges can cut other items, so wrap them in moving blankets.
- [ ] Hoses, sprinklers, watering cans: drain completely. Coil hoses tightly and secure with a bungee.
- [ ] Potted plants you want to bring: repot into plastic (not clay) for the trip. Research Oregon's plant import rules — the Oregon Department of Agriculture runs inspection stations on major highways entering the state. Generally, healthy houseplants in commercial potting soil are fine, but plants in outdoor soil, plants with visible pests, and certain species may be flagged. When in doubt, check ODA's website or call them. Many people find it simpler to give plants away and start fresh.
- [ ] Doormat, boot tray, welcome sign, porch decor
- [ ] Outdoor lighting: solar stakes, string lights, lanterns (remove batteries from battery-powered items)
- [ ] Bird feeders, garden art, wind chimes
- [ ] Hose reel or wall mount (if detachable)
- [ ] Car trunk and glovebox: clean out everything. Registration and insurance go in the documents pouch. Emergency kit stays in the car. Toss old receipts, napkins, and forgotten groceries.
- [ ] Storage unit (if you have one): ideally empty this 2–3 weeks before the move so you can sort and integrate its contents into your packing. Don't leave it for moving day — you won't have time or energy. Cancel the unit after final cleanout and get confirmation in writing.

---

## ELECTRONICS BACKUP SUMMARY

Posting this as a consolidated reference since electronics are spread across rooms.

| Device | Backup Method | Where It Rides | Pre-Move Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Desktop computer | External drive + cloud | Truck (wrapped, upright) | Remove heavy GPU, photograph cables |
| Laptop(s) | Cloud sync, verify current | Car, in your bag | Fully charge before departure |
| External hard drives | They are the backup | Car, documents pouch or bag | Label each with contents |
| Phones and tablets | iCloud / Google auto-backup | On your person | Download offline maps for route |
| Printer | n/a | Truck (or recycle) | Remove cartridges, bag them |
| Camera and lenses | Cloud or external drive for photos | Car | Note serial numbers |
| Gaming console | Cloud save if available (PS+, Xbox Live, Nintendo Online) | Truck (original box if possible) | Photograph cable setup |
| Smart home devices (thermostat, plugs, cameras) | Settings in their apps | Truck or leave behind | Reset to factory if leaving for landlord |
| Router / modem | n/a | Return if rented; truck if owned | Check ISP ownership records |
| USB drives and memory cards | Consider consolidating onto one larger drive | Car | Label every one |

---

## IMPORTANT PAPERWORK: WHAT TO PACK AND CARRY WITH YOU

Everything in this section rides in a single folder, accordion file, or zippered pouch in the car — never in the moving truck. If the truck is delayed, lost, or damaged, you need these documents accessible.

### Identity and Legal

- [ ] Driver's licenses for both of you (on your person, obviously)
- [ ] Passports (even if you're not flying — they're a universal backup ID)
- [ ] Social Security cards or a record of your numbers

turns.text:
# Important Paperwork: Complete List

*Everything in this section rides in a single folder, accordion file, or zippered pouch in the car — never in the moving truck.*

---

## CARRY WITH YOU IN THE CAR

### Identity and Legal

- [ ] Driver's licenses for both of you (on your person)
- [ ] Passports (even if you're not flying — universal backup ID and you'll need them if you decide to get an Enhanced Driver License in Oregon)
- [ ] Social Security cards or a written record of your numbers stored securely
- [ ] Birth certificates (originals or certified copies)
- [ ] Marriage certificate or domestic partnership documents, if applicable
- [ ] Immigration or naturalization documents, green cards, work visas, if applicable
- [ ] Power of attorney documents, if any exist
- [ ] Any active court orders (custody, restraining, etc.)

### Housing

- [ ] Current Ohio lease and any move-out agreement or inspection checklist
- [ ] New Oregon lease, offer letter, or closing documents
- [ ] Deposit receipts for both properties (Ohio security deposit you're owed, Oregon deposit you've paid)
- [ ] Landlord and property manager contact information for both locations
- [ ] Temporary housing confirmation (Airbnb, extended stay, hotel) with confirmation numbers

### Moving and Vehicle

- [ ] Moving company contract, estimate, and Bill of Lading (you'll sign this on moving day — keep your copy)
- [ ] Inventory list from the mover (or your own if DIY)
- [ ] Vehicle shipping contract and carrier contact info, if applicable
- [ ] DIY truck rental confirmation, if applicable
- [ ] Vehicle titles for every vehicle you own (you'll need these to register in Oregon)
- [ ] Current vehicle registrations
- [ ] Auto insurance cards and policy number
- [ ] AAA or roadside assistance membership card and number

### Financial

- [ ] Bank and credit union account numbers and customer service phone numbers (write these down — if your phone dies or is lost, you need them)
- [ ] Credit card numbers and lost/stolen reporting numbers
- [ ] Recent pay stubs (Oregon landlords and the DMV may request proof of income or residency)
- [ ] Checkbook, if you use one (some Oregon deposits, DMV fees, or utility setups still prefer checks)
- [ ] Moving expense receipts as you accumulate them (keep a running envelope)
- [ ] Renter's or homeowner's insurance policy documents and agent contact
- [ ] Health insurance cards and policy documents

### Medical

- [ ] Current prescriptions with original pharmacy labels (carry enough medication for the trip plus 2 extra weeks in case of delays)
- [ ] List of current medications, dosages, and prescribing doctors for each person
- [ ] Health insurance cards
- [ ] Copies of recent medical records if you're switching providers (or confirm your current provider can transfer electronically)
- [ ] Dental and vision records or provider contact info for transfers
- [ ] Vaccination records, if you have them handy
- [ ] Eyeglass or contact lens prescriptions

### Pet

- [ ] Rabies certificate (current, with expiration date visible)
- [ ] Vaccination records (full history, not just rabies)
- [ ] Microchip number and registry login information
- [ ] Current medication list and dosages
- [ ] Vet contact information (Ohio vet for records requests, Oregon vet for first visit)
- [ ] Recent health exam notes
- [ ] Pet insurance policy, if applicable
- [ ] Photo of your dog on your phone (in case of separation during the trip — having a recent, clear photo speeds up any search)

### Employment and Education

- [ ] Employer offer letters, relocation agreements, or remote work approvals
- [ ] Professional licenses or certifications that may need state transfer (nursing, teaching, law, real estate, cosmetology — Oregon has its own licensing boards and reciprocity varies, so research yours early)
- [ ] Transcripts or diplomas if you're applying for jobs or further education in Oregon
- [ ] Letters of recommendation you want to keep
- [ ] Union membership documents, if applicable

### Tax and Legal Reference

- [ ] Last 3 years of federal and state tax returns (digital copies on a USB drive are fine as a backup, but keep at least the most recent year in paper)
- [ ] W-2s and 1099s from the current year
- [ ] Property tax records if you own the Ohio home
- [ ] Records of your move date, mileage, and expenses (you may need these for part-year resident filings in both Ohio and Oregon)

---

## CAN GO IN THE MOVING TRUCK

These are important but not irreplaceable or urgently needed during transit. Pack them in a clearly labeled box marked "OFFICE — FILES — DO NOT LOSE."

- [ ] Older tax returns (years 3–7)
- [ ] Appliance manuals and warranty cards
- [ ] Home improvement records and receipts (if selling the Ohio house)
- [ ] Old financial statements you're keeping for reference
- [ ] Academic records and old transcripts you don't need immediately
- [ ] Sentimental letters, cards, and paper keepsakes
- [ ] Photo prints and negatives not in albums (wrap in acid-free tissue if you have it, or at minimum keep them in a sealed plastic bin to protect from moisture in the truck)
- [ ] Non-critical legal documents (old leases, closed account records, expired contracts)
- [ ] Filing cabinet contents that passed your declutter review

---

# 6–8 Week Calendar of Phone Reminders

**How to use this:** Each entry has a suggested date relative to Move Day (MD), a responsibility tag, a priority level, and a short title plus one-line body you can copy and paste directly into Google Calendar, Apple Calendar, or any reminder app. Set each one as an all-day event or a morning alert for the date listed.

Adjust dates by plugging in your actual move day. If your move day is a Saturday, count backwards from that Saturday.

---

## WEEK 8 (MD minus 56 days)

| Day | Who | Priority | Calendar Title | Body |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MD-56 | J | HIGH | Send lease termination notice | Write and deliver written notice to landlord today. Photograph or email a copy for your records. |
| MD-55 | J | HIGH | Request moving quotes | Contact 3–4 interstate movers for binding estimates. Verify USDOT numbers on FMCSA's site. |
| MD-55 | M | HIGH | Get vehicle shipping quotes | If shipping a car, request 2–3 quotes. Compare open vs enclosed. |
| MD-54 | M | HIGH | Book vet visit for dog | Schedule health check, records copy, and rabies certificate update. |
| MD-53 | J | MED | Start Oregon housing search | Set search alerts on Zillow, Apartments.com, Craigslist. Define budget and neighborhoods. |

## WEEK 7 (MD minus 49 days)

| Day | Who | Priority | Calendar Title | Body |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MD-49 | J | HIGH | Compare mover quotes and decide | Full-service, hybrid, or DIY? Review estimates, insurance options, and dates. Book this week. |
| MD-48 | M | MED | Schedule car maintenance | Oil, tires, brakes, battery, fluids. Allow lead time for any repairs before the drive. |
| MD-47 | J | HIGH | Sign Oregon lease or confirm housing | Lock down the destination. Get lease copy for your documents folder. |
| MD-46 | J | HIGH | Book internet installation in Oregon | ISP installs can take 2+ weeks to schedule. Book the earliest slot after your arrival date. |
| MD-45 | J | MED | Book temporary housing if needed | Dog-friendly Airbnb or extended stay for first 1–2 weeks if the new place isn't ready. |

## WEEK 6 (MD minus 42 days)

| Day | Who | Priority | Calendar Title | Body |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MD-42 | J | HIGH | Start garage and attic declutter | Biggest purge zone. Sort everything: keep, donate, sell, trash. Plan 3–5 hours this weekend. |
| MD-41 | J | HIGH | Run electronics backup | Back up all computers to external drive AND cloud. Photograph serial numbers. Save license keys. |
| MD-40 | P | MED | Notify employer of move date | Confirm remote work plan, relocation reimbursement, and any paperwork needed. |
| MD-39 | M | MED | Bathroom declutter | Check all expiration dates. Dispose of old meds at pharmacy take-back. Donate unopened toiletries. |
| MD-38 | J | MED | Order packing supplies | Boxes (small, medium, large, wardrobe), tape, bubble wrap, packing paper, markers. Ask stores for free boxes too. |

## WEEK 5 (MD minus 35 days)

| Day | Who | Priority | Calendar Title | Body |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MD-35 | J | HIGH | Start closet and bedroom declutter | Pull everything out of closets. Four piles: keep, donate, sell, trash. Schedule donation pickup. |
| MD-34 | P | MED | Pack kitchen wave 1 | Baking dishes, holiday dishes, small appliances, fine glassware, extra towels, cookbooks. |
| MD-33 | M | MED | Pack living room wave 1 — books | 200 books in small/medium boxes. Label and number each box. Expect 10–13 boxes at 30–40 lbs each. |
| MD-32 | M | MED | Pack office wave 1 | Reference books, printer, office supplies, filing cabinet contents, wall art, surplus cables. |
| MD-31 | J | MED | Pack attic/basement wave 1 | Holiday decor, keepsakes, archived paperwork, stored clothes, hobby supplies. Consolidate bins. |

## WEEK 4 (MD minus 28 days)

| Day | Who | Priority | Calendar Title | Body |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MD-28 | J | HIGH | File USPS change of address | Go to usps.com. Set the forwarding start date for your move day or the day after. |
| MD-27 | J | HIGH | Schedule Ohio utility shutoffs | Electric, gas, water, trash. Set final dates for the day after you leave. Get confirmation numbers. |
| MD-27 | M | HIGH | Confirm Oregon utility start dates | Electric, gas, water. Confirm internet install date. Get everything in writing or email. |
| MD-26 | P | MED | Pack bedroom wave 1 | Off-season clothes, formal wear, extra shoes, spare bedding, luggage, memorabilia, under-bed storage. |
| MD-25 | M | MED | Pack outdoor gear | Patio furniture, grill (dispose of propane tank), recreation gear, hoses, garden tools, porch items. |
| MD-24 | M | MED | Find Oregon vet and emergency vet | Book first visit for a few days after arrival. Save 24-hour emergency vet number in your phone. |

## WEEK 3 (MD minus 21 days)

| Day | Who | Priority | Calendar Title | Body |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MD-21 | J | HIGH | Notify banks, cards, and insurers of new address | Update address with every bank, credit card, insurance company, SSA, and investment account. |
| MD-20 | P | HIGH | Pack kitchen wave 2 | Most pots, pans, utensils, mugs, spice rack, pantry items. Keep 2 plates, 2 mugs, 1 skillet, 1 pot. |
| MD-19 | M | HIGH | Pack living room wave 2 | Lamps, electronics, TV, gaming console, rugs, throws, remotes. Photograph cable setups first. |
| MD-18 | P | MED | Pack bedroom wave 2 | Most hanging clothes, folded clothes, shoes, mirrors, curtains, alarm clock, fan. Keep 2 outfits out. |
| MD-17 | M | MED | Pack bathroom wave 1 | Backup toiletries, first aid kit, stored meds, extra towels, hair tools, decor, cleaning supplies, scale. |
| MD-16 | J | MED | Cancel or transfer subscriptions and services | See services checklist: gym, newspapers, meal kits, lawn care, pest control, security system, PO box. |

## WEEK 2 (MD minus 14 days)

| Day | Who | Priority | Calendar Title | Body |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MD-14 | J | HIGH | Confirm mover details | Call the mover. Confirm date, arrival window, crew size, payment method, valuation coverage. Get written confirmation. |
| MD-13 | M | HIGH | Confirm vehicle shipping pickup | If shipping: confirm date, location, carrier contact, and what to remove from the car. |
| MD-12 | M | HIGH | Update auto insurance for Oregon | Call your insurer. Confirm out-of-state coverage, update address, and ask about policy transfer. |
| MD-11 | J | MED | Sell or donate remaining declutter items | Final pickup for donations. Post last-chance items online. Anything left goes to curb or trash. |
| MD-10 | M | MED | Pack attic/basement wave 2 | Large and awkward items: folding tables, shelving, dehumidifier, washer/dryer prep. Final sweep with flashlight. |
| MD-9 | M | MED | Update dog's ID tag | Get a tag with your new phone number or Oregon address. Clip it on before the trip. |
| MD-8 | J | MED | Gather all important documents into car pouch | Use the full paperwork checklist. One folder or zippered pouch. Everything in the car, nothing in the truck. |

## WEEK 1 (MD minus 7 days)

| Day | Who | Priority | Calendar Title | Body |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MD-7 | J | HIGH | Pack everything except daily essentials | All rooms should be boxed except bedside kits, last kitchen items, last bathroom items, and cleaning supplies. |
| MD-6 | M | HIGH | Photograph valuables and serial numbers | Final pass. Every item of value gets a photo. Save to phone album and USB drive in car pouch. |
| MD-5 | J | HIGH | Defrost and clean fridge and freezer | Unplug 24 hours before the move. Donate or eat all perishable food. Wipe interior dry. |
| MD-5 | P | MED | Confirm all hotel bookings for road trip | Verify dog-friendly rooms, pet fees, check-in times. Save confirmation numbers on your phone. |
| MD-4 | M | MED | Pack office wave 2 | Desktop, monitor, keyboard, return rented router/modem, disassemble desk and chair. |
| MD-3 | M | HIGH | Confirm Ohio utility shutoffs and Oregon starts | Call each provider. Verify dates. Last chance to fix scheduling errors. |
| MD-3 | M | MED | Pack dog travel kit | Food, water, bowls, leash, poop bags, meds, vet records, blanket, favorite toy, calming aids, treats. |
| MD-2 | J | MED | Disassemble bed frame and remaining furniture | Bag all hardware, tape to furniture, photograph assembly if complex. |
| MD-1 | J | HIGH | Pack last kitchen, bathroom, and bedside items | Strip the bed. Last dishes into "OPEN FIRST" box. Bathroom final wipe. Bedside kits into the car. |
| MD-1 | J | HIGH | Assemble bedside kits and car essentials box | Chargers, meds, 2 outfits each, toiletry bag, glasses, dog travel kit, documents pouch, pillows, snacks. |

## MOVING DAY (MD)

| Time | Who | Priority | Calendar Title | Body |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Morning | J | HIGH | Moving day — walk-through photos | Photograph every room, closet, and the exterior before movers arrive. |
| Morning | J | HIGH | Review and sign Bill of Lading | Read it. Note any pre-existing damage on inventory. Keep your copy in the car pouch. |
| Midday | M | HIGH | Secure dog during loading | Crate or closed room away from movers. Familiar bed and toy. Water available. |
| Departure | J | HIGH | Return keys and do final meter read | Keys, remotes, fobs to landlord. Photograph meters. Get a receipt for keys if possible.

# MOVING DAY ESSENTIALS — CAR KIT

*Print this. Tape it to the glovebox. Check every box before you pull out of the driveway.*

---

## DOCUMENTS — **J loads, M verifies**

- [ ] Driver's licenses and passports
- [ ] Social Security cards, birth/marriage certificates
- [ ] Vehicle titles, registrations, insurance cards
- [ ] Ohio lease + move-out checklist
- [ ] Oregon lease + deposit receipts
- [ ] Moving contract, Bill of Lading, inventory copy
- [ ] Vehicle shipping contract + carrier phone number
- [ ] Dog: rabies cert, vaccine records, microchip number
- [ ] Medical prescriptions list + insurance cards
- [ ] Bank/credit card numbers + customer service phone numbers
- [ ] Employer relocation docs, if applicable
- [ ] USB drive with backups + serial number photos

---

## PERSONALS — **each person packs their own**

- [ ] Phone + charger + backup battery (x2)
- [ ] Laptop + charger
- [ ] 2 outfits each (travel day + arrival day)
- [ ] Pajamas
- [ ] Toiletry bag: toothbrush, toothpaste, deodorant, face wash, razor, contacts/glasses
- [ ] Current medications and vitamins (original labels)
- [ ] Pillow per person
- [ ] Light jacket or layers (mountain passes get cold)
- [ ] Earbuds or headphones
- [ ] Eye mask + earplugs for hotel nights
- [ ] Keys to new Oregon home

---

## DOG — **M**

- [ ] Leash, collar, harness + ID tag with new phone number
- [ ] Food (enough for travel days + 3 extra days)
- [ ] Collapsible water bowl + water bottle
- [ ] Poop bags
- [ ] Favorite toy + familiar blanket or bed
- [ ] Crate or car seatbelt harness
- [ ] Medications + calming aids if vet-recommended
- [ ] Vet records folder (copy of everything)
- [ ] Treats for rest stops
- [ ] Paper towels + enzyme cleaner for accidents

---

## CAR & TOOLS — **M**

- [ ] Jumper cables or portable jump starter
- [ ] Tire pressure gauge
- [ ] Basic toolkit: screwdriver, pliers, adjustable wrench, box cutter, tape measure
- [ ] Packing tape + Sharpie (for labeling on arrival)
- [ ] Flashlight or headlamp
- [ ] First aid kit
- [ ] Spare tire confirmed + jack + lug wrench
- [ ] Windshield washer fluid
- [ ] Ice scraper if crossing passes in cool months
- [ ] Paper maps or printed route (backup for dead zones)
- [ ] Roadside assistance number saved in phone

---

## SNACKS & COMFORT — **P**

- [ ] Water bottles (refillable, filled)
- [ ] Cooler with drinks and perishable snacks
- [ ] Non-perishable snacks: granola bars, nuts, dried fruit, crackers
- [ ] Napkins + wet wipes
- [ ] Trash bag clipped to seat back
- [ ] Sunglasses (x2)
- [ ] Sunscreen
- [ ] Downloaded playlists, podcasts, audiobooks (cell gaps in WY/ID/OR)
- [ ] Blanket for the back seat

---

## MONEY & PAYMENTS — **J**

- [ ] Wallet with debit/credit cards
- [ ] Cash: $200–$300 small bills (tips for movers, tolls, emergencies, rural gas stations)
- [ ] Mover payment method confirmed (cashier's check, card, or money order — many movers don't accept personal checks at delivery)
- [ ] Venmo/Zelle loaded for incidentals
- [ ] Receipts envelope for tax/reimbursement records

---

### CAR PACKING ORDER

**1. Trunk floor first:** toolbox, jumper cables, first aid kit, cleaning supplies, cooler flat against the back wall.
**2. Trunk top layer:** dog crate or bed, suitcases with clothes, pillows, blanket, snack bag.
**3. Back seat + footwells:** documents pouch within driver's reach, dog travel kit, laptops in bags, "OPEN FIRST — KITCHEN" box if it fits, trash bag hooked to headrest.

Happy with how it all came together. You now have the full set:

The phased master checklist from 10 weeks out through post-move, room-by-room packing guides for every space in the house, the electronics backup protocol, the complete documents list (car vs. truck), the 6–8 week calendar of phone reminders ready to paste into your calendar app, and the printable one-page car kit checklist.

Whenever you're ready, I can help with any of these next steps: the services and subscriptions cancel/start checklist (gym, streaming, utilities, insurance transfers — everything in one list with timing), a detailed driving route plan with dog-friendly stops, lodging, and rest breaks across Ohio to Oregon, a final budget spreadsheet template you can plug your real quotes into, or customizing any of the responsibility assignments or timelines now that you've looked it over together.

Just say the word.
